section.title: The Futility of Wealth
section.sectionRationale: Having warned about rash words before God, the Teacher turns to money. He watches the machinery of oppression grind on, exposes the restless hunger of the money lover, and traces wealth to its bitter ends: it robs sleep, it can be hoarded to a man's harm or lost in a bad venture, and it slips from naked hands at death. Then, without softening any of it, he lifts his eyes and names the one thing that changes everything, the ability to enjoy God's gifts as gifts from God's hand.
section.thesis: Money can never satisfy the heart that loves it, and none of it survives the grave; yet the same God who exposes wealth as futile gives, to those He chooses, the power to eat, drink, and rejoice in their labor as His gift.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the oppression no one escapes and the endless hunger for more; the grievous evil of wealth that harms or vanishes and leaves us as naked as we came; and the turn to joy, the God given gift of enjoying our lot.

units.label: Oppression and the hunger for more

verses.text: If you see the oppression of the poor and the denial of justice and righteousness in the province, do not be astonished at the matter; for one official is watched by a superior, and others higher still are over them.
The produce of the earth is taken by all; the king himself profits from the fields.
He who loves money is never satisfied by money, and he who loves wealth is never satisfied by income. This too is {{hevel|futile}}.
When good things increase, so do those who consume them; what then is the {{yitron|profit}} to the owner, except to behold them with his eyes?
The sleep of the worker is sweet, whether he eats little or much, but the abundance of the rich man permits him no sleep.

units.label: Wealth that harms and vanishes
units.note: naked we came, naked we go

verses.text: There is a grievous evil I have seen under the sun: wealth hoarded to the harm of its owner,
or wealth lost in a failed venture, so when that man has a son there is nothing to pass on.
As a man came from his mother’s womb, so he will depart again, naked as he arrived. He takes nothing for his labor to carry in his hands.
This too is a grievous affliction: Exactly as a man is born, so he will depart. What does he {{yitron|gain}} as he {{amal|toils}} for the wind?
Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness, with much sorrow, sickness, and anger.

units.label: The gift of enjoyment
units.note: receive your lot from God's hand

verses.text: Here is what I have seen to be good and fitting: to eat and drink, and to find satisfaction in all the labor one does under the sun during the few days of life that God has given him, for this is his lot.
Furthermore, God has given riches and wealth to every man, and He has enabled him to enjoy them, to accept his lot, and to rejoice in his labor. This is a gift from God.
For a man seldom considers the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart.

hevel.gloss: Vapor, breath, mist, the word that drums through Ecclesiastes as 'vanity' or 'futile.' It does not mean worthless so much as fleeting, insubstantial, impossible to grasp or hold. Money loved for its own sake is hevel: you reach for it and close your hand on breath.

amal.gloss: Toil, labor, the wearying work by which we make a living, often with a note of trouble or grievance. To toil for the wind is to pour out a lifetime of effort and end with empty hands.

yitron.gloss: Gain, profit, advantage, what is left over when the accounts are settled. It is a favorite question of the Teacher: what real, lasting yitron does a man have from all his toil under the sun? Wealth adds up to no surplus you can carry past the grave.

basic.context: The Teacher looks hard at money and the world it runs. He is not naive: he sees officials preying on the poor, layer upon layer of them, and a system where everyone, up to the king, feeds off the land. Then he exposes the secret of wealth: it never satisfies the person who loves it. The more you have, the more people gather to spend it, the less you sleep, and in the end you leave the world exactly as you entered it, naked, carrying nothing. Yet he does not stop in despair. He names a genuine good: to eat, drink, and enjoy your work as a gift from God.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage is realistic wisdom, not a rule to renounce all possessions. It describes the world as it actually is 'under the sun,' where wealth cannot fill the soul or survive death. The key turn is verses 18 to 20: the same things that are futile when clutched become good when received as God's gift. The difference is not the amount of money but whether it is grasped apart from God or accepted from His hand with thanks.
basic.originalLanguages: Two Hebrew words carry the weight. Hevel, breath or vapor, is the refrain 'futile': money loved for itself is like grasping at mist. Yitron is 'gain' or 'profit,' the surplus left when the accounting is done, and the Teacher keeps asking what real gain a man has from his toil, amal, his wearying labor. The answer under the sun is: none you can keep. The only gain that lasts is the joy God gives.
basic.typology: The picture of coming naked from the womb and departing naked points ahead to the truth Paul draws out, that we brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out. The 'gift' of enjoyment given by God's hand anticipates the fuller gift of the gospel, where God gives us His Son and, with Him, all things to enjoy.
basic.christ: Wealth cannot satisfy or save; it leaves us empty handed at death. Jesus warns of the man who stored up treasure and lost his soul, and calls us to be rich toward God. He is the one who, though rich, became poor so that we through His poverty might become rich. The enjoyment of daily bread as God's gift finds its home in Him, who teaches us to pray for daily bread and gives us Himself as the bread of life.
basic.god: God stands over the whole scene. He is the giver: riches, wealth, and, more importantly, the very power to enjoy them come from His hand. He is generous, wanting His people to eat, drink, and rejoice. And He alone can quiet the restless heart, keeping a person occupied with the joy of his heart so the days do not feel like a burden.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Timothy 6 warns that the love of money is a root of evil, echoing 'naked we came.' Luke 12 tells of the rich fool who was not rich toward God. Matthew 6 says we cannot serve God and money. James 5 rebukes hoarded wealth that rots.
basic.oneStory: In a fallen world, wealth is hevel, breath that cannot fill the soul or cross the grave. But the Teacher points past the money to the Giver, and the whole Bible follows that finger to Christ, who alone satisfies and who gives us all things, including the simple joy of daily bread, as gifts to be received from a Father's hand.

context.literary:
Ecclesiastes 5 changes gear in verse 8. The first seven verses were about the sanctuary and the tongue, with their steady refrain of caution before God. Now the Teacher turns to the marketplace and the treasury. The passage that follows reads as three panels, and each one ends by pressing on the word 'all' or 'nothing'. In the first panel, verses 8 to 12, the hunger for money is traced from the top of the administrative pyramid down to the bedroom of the rich man who cannot sleep. In the second, verses 13 to 17, the Teacher says 'I have seen' and produces a case study, a fortune that is kept and destroys its owner, or risked and lost, and either way ends in the same naked departure. The third panel, verses 18 to 20, opens with the phrase 'Here is what I have seen to be good', a deliberate echo of the 'I have seen' that began the case study, so the two verdicts stand side by side.

The passage is carried by repetition. 'Money' and 'wealth' are heaped up in verses 10 and 11, and then the ledger vocabulary of the first chapters returns in verse 16, 'what does he gain as he toils for the wind?' That question is a deliberate rerun of the book's opening, Ecclesiastes 1:3. The word 'eat' is also a quiet thread: the many who consume the owner's goods in verse 11, the man who eats in darkness in verse 17, and the man who is commended for eating and drinking in verse 18. Eating is the one place where wealth touches the body, and the Teacher uses it to separate the futile kind of having from the gifted kind.

The unit also belongs to a larger pattern. The book places a short enjoyment passage at the close of several movements, at 2:24 to 26, 3:12 to 13, 3:22, and here at 5:18 to 20, each time after a hard observation. This one is the fullest so far, with its three words for God's giving ('given', 'enabled', 'gift') packed into two verses. It also sets up chapter 6, which will reopen the same wound from the opposite side.
context.historical:
The picture in verses 8 and 9 is of a province under layered administration, and the word for 'province' in verse 8 is the one the Teacher also used when listing his treasures in Ecclesiastes 2:8. Whether the book is read as coming from Solomon's court or from a later, imperial age, its first hearers knew a system in which a tax, a tithe or a levy passed upward through officials, each answerable to the next. Verse 9 is among the hardest verses in the book to translate, and some versions take it to say that a land with a king over it is good for everyone, because the produce is organised and defended. The BSB reads it more darkly, that even the king draws profit from the fields. Either way, the Teacher's advice not to be 'astonished' recognises that a cry for justice reaches no end, because there is always a higher official to blame.

Money in this world was not the abstract thing it is now. Wealth was grain in storehouses, silver weighed on scales, flocks and land, and it was kept in jars or buried. That explains the fear of verses 13 and 14. A hoard could be stolen, a ship or a caravan could be lost, and a son who expected an inheritance could be left with an empty hand. The prophets show the other side of the same economy: those who 'add house to house and join field to field', Isaiah 5:8, and who 'covet fields and seize them', Micah 2:2.

The nakedness of verse 15 also carries a Near Eastern flavour. Burial with wealth was common in the great kingdoms around Israel, and the grave goods of Egyptian kings were meant to be carried into the next life. The Teacher says plainly that no such luggage exists. A man will leave his mother's womb with empty hands, and he will leave the world in the same way, a line Job also spoke at the lowest moment of his life, Job 1:21.
context.canonical:
The Torah had already taught that wealth is a gift to be received and remembered, never an achievement to be admired. When Israel was about to enter a land of ease, Moses warned them not to say 'The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me', because 'it is the LORD your God who gives you the power to gain wealth', Deuteronomy 8:17 to 18. Ecclesiastes 5:19 reads like a sermon on that verse, and it uses a related thought: God gives not only the riches but the capacity to enjoy them.

The wisdom books handle the same ground from different angles. Proverbs asks for neither poverty nor riches, only 'the bread that is my portion', and gives the reason, that too much might lead to the denial of God, Proverbs 30:8 to 9. Proverbs 23:4 to 5 says wealth 'makes wings for itself and flies like an eagle to the sky'. Psalm 49:16 to 20 says almost word for word what Ecclesiastes 5:15 says: a rich man will 'carry nothing away' when he dies. Psalm 127:2 gives the sleep of verse 12 a theology, because it is God who gives sleep to His beloved, and anxious toil cannot buy it.

In the New Testament the passage is taken up directly. Paul writes that 'we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it', and that 'godliness with contentment is great gain', 1 Timothy 6:6 to 7, the same ledger word, 'gain', that the Teacher keeps using. A few verses later, Paul tells the rich to put their hope 'in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy', 1 Timothy 6:17, which is the Teacher's verse 19 in the language of the church. Jesus' parable of the rich fool in Luke 12:16 to 21 dramatises verses 13 to 15, and His warning about treasures on earth in Matthew 6:19 to 21 addresses the same fear of loss.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Teacher wants his hearers to stop being impressed. Verse 8 is aimed at the person who watches injustice and is shocked by it, and who thinks that if the right official were reached, the problem would be fixed. He tells them it is a system, with hands in every pocket up to the throne. That does not mean they should shrug at wrong; other books of the Bible demand justice loudly. It means they should not stake their peace on the world getting fairer, and they should not stake their joy on getting more out of it.

The second thing he wants them to see is that wealth is a worse master than it looks. He is not writing to the poor to console them. He is writing to the person who is gaining, and warning that the gaining does not end. The proverb of verse 10 is meant to be repeated as a test, a way of asking oneself whether the last raise or the last sale actually quieted anything.

Then he wants them to take a posture. The verses about the 'lot' and the 'gift' are not an afterthought to console the reader after bad news. They are the point the bad news has been preparing. If wealth cannot be kept and cannot satisfy, the only sane use of it is to enjoy it today as a gift, with thanks, and with a lightness of hand that lets it go when it must.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 8 to 17 are almost entirely observation. The Teacher reports an oppressive bureaucracy, a restless rich man, a hoard that hurts and a bad investment, without once saying that any of it is acceptable. Treating 'do not be astonished' as permission to tolerate oppression would be a serious mistake. The law and the prophets condemn what verse 8 describes: the poor are not to be oppressed, and the Lord is the defender of the weak, Proverbs 14:31 and Psalm 82:3 to 4. The Teacher is describing the limits of what can be fixed by the officials, not retiring the believer's duty to act.

The nearest thing to a command is in verses 18 to 20, and even there it is stated as something he has seen to be 'good and fitting'. That gives it a gentle authority. It does not tell the poor to be grateful for oppression, and it does not tell the rich to hoard and call it a gift. What carries forward is the pattern of receiving, working, eating and giving thanks. Where the Teacher's remarks are about the whole lifetime of a hearer, the New Testament turns them into direct instruction: be content, trust God rather than riches, and be generous, 1 Timothy 6:6 to 19.

debates.question: Does 'God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart' in verse 20 mean God distracts, or God answers?

views.label: God keeps him occupied
views.case: This is how the BSB and many versions take it. The same verb in Ecclesiastes 1:13 and 3:10 describes the 'task' God has given people to be busy with. On this reading verse 20 says a person who receives God's gift is so absorbed in gladness that the brevity of life does not weigh him down.

views.label: God answers him in the joy of his heart
views.case: The older English versions, such as the King James, took the verb as 'answer'. On that reading, joy is God's reply to the person, a sign that God is attending to him. This fits the biblical pattern that God answers those who seek Him, and it reads verse 20 as comfort rather than distraction.

views.label: God distracts, so that he does not brood
views.case: Some take the verse more darkly. The man who dwells on the shortness of his days would be crushed, so God diverts him with enjoyment. The joy is real, but its function is to dull the pain of knowing that days are few.

debates.bearing: The grammar allows all three, and the book's wider habit favours the first or second. In 2:24 to 25 and 3:13 the Teacher says enjoyment is the hand of God at work, not a narcotic. The darker reading sits awkwardly with calling the joy a 'gift from God' in verse 19, so the most natural reading is that God is gently occupying the person with real gladness.

debates.question: Is the Teacher commending enjoyment as the best life has to offer, or as a pointer to something beyond itself?

views.label: Enjoyment is the best available
views.case: The phrase 'under the sun' marks a horizon that stops at the grave, and within that horizon the Teacher says nothing is better than eating, drinking and rejoicing in labour. On this reading the book is honest wisdom for a world without a visible afterlife, and the passage is a concession, not a promise.

views.label: Enjoyment is a God given sign pointing beyond itself
views.case: The passage insists that it is 'a gift from God' and that God 'enabled' it, so the pleasure is never self contained. The New Testament takes it that way, saying God gives all things 'for us to enjoy', 1 Timothy 6:17, and that earthly gifts are meant to lead to thanks and then to hope in the Giver.

debates.bearing: Both are true at the level of the book. Within its own horizon the Teacher offers enjoyment as the best that can be held, but he never makes it an idol, since it comes from God's hand. In the whole canon, the gift points to the Giver, and the Giver has promised more than a few days under the sun.

study.originalLanguages:
Several words in this passage carry more than a translation can show. The first is the verb that closes verse 10. The money lover is 'never satisfied', and the root for satisfaction here is the ordinary word for being full after a meal, the same sense it has in Psalm 107:9, where the Lord 'satisfies the thirsty and fills the hungry with good things'. The Teacher uses the language of appetite for money, and he is right to, because the Bible keeps comparing greed to hunger, as in Habakkuk 2:5, where the arrogant man 'enlarges his appetite like Sheol, and like Death, he is never satisfied'. In Hebrew thought, then, greed is not a failure of arithmetic. It is an appetite, and no quantity of bread will cure an appetite that has mistaken coins for bread.

The second is the phrase 'grievous evil' in verses 13 and 16. The adjective is related to the word for illness, so the phrase can be read as a 'sick evil' or a 'sickening evil', and the Teacher is speaking of the money problem as a disease that damages its victim from within. When he uses the same kind of language at the start of chapter 6, 'it weighs heavily upon mankind', he is naming it a common sickness, not a rare tragedy.

The third is the 'failed venture' of verse 14. The Hebrew word for business or occupation is the same word the Teacher used for the 'task' God has given people to be busy with, Ecclesiastes 1:13 and 3:10. A bad 'venture' is a kind of 'bad business', and the Teacher is quietly hinting that every human enterprise, however sensible, is subject to a God who can overturn it.

The fourth is 'lot', the Hebrew cheleq, meaning a portion or share. It is the word for the land allotment given to each tribe, and it is used in Deuteronomy 10:9 for what Levi did not receive: 'Levi has no portion or inheritance among his brothers; the LORD is his inheritance'. In the Psalms, the word becomes a confession of faith: 'The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; You have made my lot secure', Psalm 16:5. In Ecclesiastes 5:18 and 5:19 the 'lot' is the share God hands to each person, and the Teacher's counsel is to accept it as it comes, with joy, rather than hunger for someone else's.

The fifth is the verb behind 'He has enabled him to enjoy them' in verse 19. It is built on a root that normally means to rule or have power over. The Teacher chooses a word of authority to speak of enjoyment: God gives a person the power, the mastery, to enjoy what he has. In 6:2, when the same root is used negatively, God 'does not allow' a man to enjoy his goods. The same family of words is used in 8:4, where the king's word is 'supreme', and in 8:8, where no one has 'authority' over the day of death. Taken together, the book is saying that real authority over a person's life, including over his capacity for happiness, belongs to God.

Finally, 'a gift from God', mattat elohim, is a phrase the book uses more than once, in 3:13 and here. It makes enjoyment a grace, not a wage, and it matches the Hebrew sense of 'gift' as something given without being earned.

typology.type: Manna: a daily portion that cannot be hoarded, Exodus 16
typology.fulfillment: Israel was told to gather only what was needed for the day, and what was kept until morning 'became infested with maggots and began to smell', Exodus 16:19 to 20. That is verse 13's hoarded wealth in a desert setting: the portion that is kept to excess spoils. Jesus takes the manna as a sign of Himself, 'I am the bread of life', John 6:35, and teaches His people to ask for daily bread, Matthew 6:11. The fulfilment goes beyond the type, since manna fed the body for a day, while the true bread gives life that does not end. The type falls short because manna was only a sign and the generation that ate it still died.

typology.type: The Levite whose portion is the LORD, Deuteronomy 10:9
typology.fulfillment: The tribe of Levi received no land, because the LORD was their inheritance, Numbers 18:20. They lived on what God provided through the offerings, and their security lay in His promise, not in an estate. This is the 'lot' of Ecclesiastes 5:18 at its purest. In Christ, the whole people of God now share in that inheritance, 'heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ', Romans 8:17, and Peter speaks of an inheritance 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading', 1 Peter 1:4. The type falls short because the Levite's portion depended on the temple system and the people's faithfulness, but the believer's portion is held in Christ.

typology.type: The heir who receives nothing, versus the Son appointed heir of all things
typology.fulfillment: Verse 14 pictures a man with a son but nothing to pass on. Hebrews opens with a Son 'whom He appointed heir of all things', Hebrews 1:2, and Paul says that those in Christ are heirs with Him, Romans 8:17. The relationship runs in the opposite direction from verse 14: the rich Son became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9, so that His people would not be left without an inheritance. The correspondence is real, but Christ does not merely keep wealth for His family. He gives Himself, and the inheritance is not subject to bad ventures, because it is 'reserved in heaven', 1 Peter 1:4.

Job said, 'Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I will return', and he said it in worship. The Teacher says it in sober observation, and Paul in a warning. Christ's own life follows the pattern in a way that is almost unbearable: He was wrapped in strips of cloth at birth, Luke 2:7, stripped of His garments at the cross, John 19:23 to 24, and laid in a tomb that belonged to a rich man, Matthew 27:57 to 60, and Isaiah 53:9. The pattern is fulfilled when He rises, leaving the burial cloths behind. The type falls short in that Job could only submit, while Christ goes through nakedness and out the other side.

study.christ:
Christ meets this passage first as the one who lived what it describes. He was born into a feeding trough, Luke 2:7, and said that the Son of Man had nowhere to lay His head, Luke 9:58. He did not hold the world's wealth, though 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich', 2 Corinthians 8:9. The Teacher says a man leaves with empty hands. Jesus died with His clothes divided by lot, John 19:23 to 24, and was buried in a borrowed tomb, Matthew 27:57 to 60. He is the one man who could have had everything and who spent it all on others.

He is also the teacher of the same truths. 'Watch out! Guard yourselves against every form of greed, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions', Luke 12:15, introduces the rich fool, who plans larger barns and hears 'This very night your life will be required of you. Then who will own what you have accumulated?' That last question is verse 14 given a face. In Mark 8:36 He asks, 'What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul?', which uses the language of profit that the Teacher has made central to the book. When the rich young man went away sad, Jesus said it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom, and when the disciples asked who could be saved, He answered, 'With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible', Matthew 19:23 to 26. That is the gospel's answer to the problem of wealth: the grip on money cannot be loosened by effort, and God does it by grace.

Christ also fulfils the longing of verse 12 for sleep. The Lord who sleeps in a storm, Mark 4:38, invites the weary to come to Him for rest, Matthew 11:28. He promises to His people, 'Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father is pleased to give you the kingdom', Luke 12:32, so the anxious accumulation of verses 10 to 17 is replaced with the kind of trust that sleeps.

The passage, finally, sets up the gospel's offer of an inheritance that cannot be lost. The man in verse 14 has no inheritance to leave his son. The believer, by contrast, is a co-heir with Christ, Romans 8:17, and his inheritance is 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading', 1 Peter 1:4. A caution is needed. It would be a mistake to read every detail of the Teacher's observations as a hidden portrait of Jesus. The links here run through the New Testament's own words about wealth, poverty and inheritance, and not through allegory.
study.god:
The central teaching of the passage about God is that He is the giver, and that He gives in two layers. He gives the thing, 'riches and wealth', and He gives the power to enjoy the thing. Verse 19 says it twice, in 'God has given riches' and 'He has enabled him to enjoy them'. The second gift is the rarer and the more necessary, because a man can possess everything and still be unable to taste it, as chapter 6 will show. That means enjoyment is not a technique and not a personality trait. It is a grace, and the God who gives bread also gives appetite for it.

The passage also shows God as the one who stands above the pyramid. Verse 8 describes official above official, 'and others higher still are over them'. The Hebrew can be taken to mean that the highest of these is not the end of the chain. Elsewhere the Bible says plainly who is above every ruler: 'God presides in the divine assembly; He renders judgment among the gods', Psalm 82:1, and He is the one who hears the cry of the oppressed, Psalm 82:3 to 4. The helplessness the Teacher describes is real, but it is not final, because the chain of accountability does not end with a human being. This is the same God who 'is in heaven' while we are 'on earth', Ecclesiastes 5:2.

There is another truth about God here, which is that He is generous. A reader of verses 13 to 17 might conclude that the world is a place where everything that is gained is stolen. Verses 18 to 20 insist otherwise. God has given 'the few days of life', and He has given the lot, the labour and the joy. The same God who has made the world a place where wealth is not a source of lasting security has also put real good in it. The Teacher is neither a pessimist about creation nor a naive optimist about what people do with it.

God is also sovereign over the economy of gifts and losses. Verse 14 treats a loss as something that happens, and does not say God caused it, but the book's frame elsewhere is clear that nothing happens outside His rule. Job's confession is the fullest statement of this: 'The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD', Job 1:21. It holds together what the book keeps asking us to hold together, that God can take away and is still to be blessed.

For worship this means that thanksgiving at a meal is a theological act, and not mere politeness. To eat and drink and give thanks is to confess that the table, the work behind it, and the appetite for it all come from God's hand, which is what the Teacher calls the lot. It also means that generosity is natural to the believer, because the one who has received everything as a gift is free to give. Paul's instruction is that the rich should be 'generous and ready to share, treasuring up for themselves a firm foundation for the future', 1 Timothy 6:18 to 19.

crossReferences.note: Moses warns Israel against saying that the power of their own hands made their wealth, and tells them it is the LORD who gives the power to gain it. This is the background for Ecclesiastes 5:19, where God gives both the riches and the ability to enjoy them. Wealth is received, not manufactured.

Job speaks the line of Ecclesiastes 5:15 almost exactly, 'Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I will return', but he says it in worship, having lost everything. It shows that the same truth can drive a man to despair or to blessing the name of the LORD.

The psalmist tells his hearers not to be amazed when a man grows rich, because at death 'he will carry nothing away'. It is the same argument as Ecclesiastes 5:15, put as a word of comfort to the people who envy the rich or fear them.

Agur asks God for neither poverty nor riches, only the bread that is his portion, because too much might make him deny the LORD and too little might make him steal. It is the proverbial counterpart to the 'lot' of Ecclesiastes 5:18, where a measured portion received from God is the safest place to be.

Anxious toil and sleeplessness are met with the statement that God gives sleep to His beloved. It supplies the theology behind Ecclesiastes 5:12, where the labourer sleeps sweetly and the rich man cannot, since rest is a gift of God and not a reward of wealth.

Paul says godliness with contentment is great gain, that we brought nothing into the world and can carry nothing out, and that the love of money pierces people with many sorrows. This is the New Testament form of Ecclesiastes 5:10 to 17, with the Teacher's word 'gain' turned into a positive.

Paul tells the rich not to hope in the uncertainty of wealth but in God, who richly provides everything for our enjoyment, and to be generous. This is Ecclesiastes 5:19 in the language of the church, and it shows the Teacher's gift of enjoyment leading directly into generosity.

Jesus warns that life does not consist in the abundance of possessions, then tells of a man who plans bigger barns and loses his life that night. The question 'who will own what you have accumulated?' is Ecclesiastes 5:14 and 15 in parable form, with the added edge of being 'not rich toward God'.

Manna kept past its day was ruined, and each person gathered only what was needed. The story gives an early picture of the limits of hoarding and of living from a daily portion, which is the shape of the 'lot' the Teacher commends in Ecclesiastes 5:18.

The first of the book's enjoyment passages says that eating, drinking and finding satisfaction in work are from God's hand, and adds the key question, 'apart from Him, who can eat and who can find enjoyment?' Chapter 5 returns to that point and sets it against wealth that cannot be enjoyed.

Jesus says not to store treasure where moth and rust destroy, but in heaven, because the heart follows the treasure. It answers the fear of loss in Ecclesiastes 5:13 and 14 by moving the treasure to a place a bad venture cannot reach.

The writer says to keep life free from the love of money and be content, because God has promised never to leave or forsake His people. This gives the Teacher's contentment its ground: it is not resignation, but trust in a God who stays.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a garden in which everything needed was given, and the one limit God set was the tree of knowledge, Genesis 2:16 to 17. The first sin was a grasp for more than had been given, a reaching for something that God had withheld, so it is no surprise that Ecclesiastes 5 describes the human condition after Eden as a hunger that more cannot satisfy. The curse of toil, Genesis 3:17 to 19, explains the Teacher's word 'toils'. The sentence on mankind, 'for dust you are and to dust you will return', explains why the owner of a hoard leaves with nothing. Everything the passage says about money is the economic side of the fall.

The story of Israel then takes the same lesson into history. Israel is brought out of slavery into a land of plenty, and warned that prosperity will tempt them to say 'My power made this', Deuteronomy 8:17. The prophets show Israel doing precisely what verse 8 describes, with leaders who oppress and landowners who add field to field, Isaiah 5:8 and Micah 2:2. The exile that follows is, among other things, the loss of the land the hoarders had grabbed. The remnant is described as those who trust the LORD and need nothing else.

What the passage prepares is the coming of a king who does not take but gives. Jesus is born poor, teaches that life does not consist in possessions, and takes up the question of the heart's treasure at the centre of the Sermon on the Mount. The first Christians are described as holding possessions loosely, Acts 2:44 to 45, not because a rule demanded it but because they had received something that made the rest secondary. The early church's teaching on contentment, and on the sin of treating wealth as a refuge, grows directly out of this soil.

The passage ends, as the Bible does, by promising that the best things are gifts. In the new creation, nobody will toil for the wind, because 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain' will remain, Revelation 21:4. The thirsty are invited to the water of life freely, Revelation 22:17, the exact reversal of the market that grinds in verses 8 to 17. The tree of life will bear fruit every month, Revelation 22:2, and the meal that the Teacher can only commend in small portions will become the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. Where the Teacher says that the only thing which goes with a person is the gladness God has given, the new creation says that gladness will be the whole of the inheritance.

quiz.q: What does the Teacher say about the person who loves money?

options.text: He is never satisfied by money or income; the craving is never filled.
options.note: Verse 10 states plainly that the money lover is never satisfied.

options.text: He tends to lose sleep because of his abundance.
options.note: True of the rich man in verse 12, but the central point is that love of money never satisfies.

options.text: He will always be punished by the king.
options.note: The passage speaks of officials and the king, but not of punishing the money lover.

options.text: He eventually finds full contentment if he earns enough.
options.note: The opposite of the text: no amount ever satisfies the one who loves it.

quiz.q: What point is made by coming from the womb and departing naked, 5:15?

options.text: We take nothing with us at death; wealth cannot cross the grave.
options.note: The naked departure shows that no gain from toil can be carried out of life.

options.text: Our labor for wealth is like toiling for the wind.
options.note: A faithful echo, verse 16, though the image itself is about leaving with empty hands.

options.text: Children inherit nothing when a venture fails.
options.note: That is verse 14's case; verse 15 is the wider truth that we all leave naked.

options.text: Wealth is evenly shared among all people.
options.note: The passage says the opposite; wealth is uneven and, in the end, unkeepable.

quiz.q: According to verses 18 to 20, what makes eating, drinking, and working good rather than futile?

options.text: Receiving them as a gift from God, with the God given power to enjoy them.
options.note: The turn is that God gives both the wealth and the ability to enjoy it as His gift.

options.text: Simply choosing to be content with one's lot in life.
options.note: Contentment is involved, but the text roots it specifically in God's gift, not mere resolve.

options.text: Working harder so there is more to enjoy.
options.note: The passage does not tie joy to greater output but to God's gift.

options.text: Giving all wealth away so none of it can harm you.
options.note: The Teacher commends enjoying God's gifts, not renouncing all possessions.

quiz.q: Is wealth itself condemned in this passage?

options.text: No; the danger is loving and clutching it, while in 5:19 riches and the power to enjoy them are called God's gift.
options.note: The problem is the grasping heart, not possession as such.

options.text: Wealth is portrayed mostly as a trap that harms its owner.
options.note: The dark side is real, 5:13 to 17, but 5:19 keeps wealth as a possible gift from God.

options.text: Only the wealth of kings and officials is condemned.
options.note: The critique is broader, aimed at the love of money in anyone.

options.text: Yes, all owning of property is treated as sin.
options.note: The text never forbids possessions; it warns against loving them and commends enjoying them as gifts.

quiz.q: How does this passage point to Christ?

options.text: It exposes wealth's emptiness and the naked grave, driving us to the true riches and daily bread found in Christ.
options.note: Jesus warns against storing treasure on earth and offers Himself as the treasure that lasts.

options.text: It teaches us to be content, which Jesus also commends.
options.note: True, but it undersells the deeper line to Christ who became poor to make us rich.

options.text: It predicts that the Messiah would be wealthy.
options.note: The passage points the other way, to the One who became poor for us.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ at all.
options.note: Its theme of true riches and received gifts runs straight to the gospel.

questions: The Teacher says the money lover is never satisfied. Where do you catch yourself believing that a little more, income, savings, security, will finally be enough?
Wealth here robs sleep and slips from naked hands at death. What are you holding so tightly that it has begun to hold you?

Verse 19 calls the power to enjoy God's gifts a gift in itself. Can you name simple things, a meal, a day's work, rest, that you could receive today as gifts from God's hand rather than take for granted?
The passage warns against clutching, not against having. Where might God be inviting you to hold your possessions more loosely and your Giver more closely?
Jesus offers treasure that death cannot touch. What would change this week if you spent yourself building that treasure instead of toiling for the wind?

translationNotes.note: The word rendered 'futile' is hevel, literally breath or vapor. It pictures money loved for itself as something you reach for and cannot hold, fleeting rather than simply worthless.
'Under the sun' is the Teacher's recurring phrase for life viewed within this world alone. 'Toils for the wind' renders amal, wearying labor, spent on what cannot be kept.
'This is a gift from God' translates language that makes enjoyment itself God's grant, not the person's achievement.
